scams.name: Taxi Bill-Switch and Counterfeit Change
scams.description:
You flag a taxi outside your hotel on Avenida 4 in El Rodadero and agree on a fare. The driver is friendly, knows the landmarks, and the trip is quick. You hand over a 20,000-peso note for a 10,000-peso fare — or a 50,000-peso note when you have nothing smaller.

The driver turns briefly toward the window or leans toward the glove compartment. When he faces you again, he is holding a 2,000-peso note and insisting you only gave him 2,000 — your bill has been palmed and the switch is already done. In the counterfeit variant, he returns your 50,000-peso note claiming it is damaged or fake. The next time you try to spend it, a shop owner tells you it is counterfeit. Your real note is long gone.

Carry small bills and pay the exact fare while stating the denomination out loud as you hand it over: 'Here is ten thousand pesos.' If you only have large notes, tell the driver before you get in so there is no ambiguity later. Ride-hailing apps — InDriver and Didi both work in Santa Marta — lock the fare digitally before you move and eliminate the cash exchange entirely.
scams.avoidance: Carry small bills (5,000 and 10,000 peso notes) and pay with exact change whenever possible State the denomination out loud as you hand it to the driver: 'Here is twenty thousand pesos' Agree on the fare before entering the taxi and have the exact amount ready Use ride-hailing apps like InDriver, Didi, or Uber where payment is handled digitally Familiarize yourself with Colombian bill denominations and security features before arriving — check returned bills for watermarks
scams.location: Taxis throughout Santa Marta, especially outside hotels in El Rodadero, the Centro Histórico, and near Parque de los Novios at night
scams.tldr: Santa Marta taxi drivers targeting tourists on routes from El Rodadero to the Centro Histórico pocket your large-denomination note while substituting a smaller bill — or return your genuine 50,000-peso note labeled counterfeit after swapping in a fake — leaving victims short 10,000 to 50,000 pesos per ride.

scams.name: Fake Police Document Inspection
scams.description:
You are walking near Parque de los Novios or along a quiet street toward Taganga when two men step toward you. They carry badges and wear dark trousers, official-looking shirts, and lanyards. Their tone is authoritative — they say they are checking tourists for counterfeit currency and need to see your documents and wallet immediately.

One man takes your passport and examines it slowly, reading each page aloud and asking questions about your itinerary. The other takes your wallet and flips through the bills, apparently checking watermarks. By the time your passport is returned and your wallet handed back, several thousand-peso notes have been removed. They give you a handwritten receipt and direct you to a police station to reclaim the cash — where real officers tell you the entire encounter was a scam.

Real Colombian police do not conduct currency inspections on the street — if anyone in uniform asks to inspect your wallet, firmly decline and offer to walk together to the nearest station instead. Scammers will evaporate at that suggestion. Leave your passport in the hotel safe and carry only a photocopy of the photo page and entry stamps. If you are genuinely stopped, hold your own documents rather than handing them over.
scams.avoidance: Leave your passport at the hotel safe and carry only a photocopy of the photo page and entry stamps If approached by supposed police, politely request to see their official photo ID and badge number Suggest walking to the nearest police station to verify their identity — real officers will agree, scammers will not Never hand over your wallet — if asked for ID, hold it yourself and let them look at it in your hands Call 123 (Colombian police emergency) to verify any officer's identity before complying with demands
scams.location: Streets around the Centro Histórico, Parque de los Novios, walkways near Taganga, and roads near popular tourist sites
scams.tldr: Pairs of men in police-like uniforms approach tourists near Parque de los Novios and Taganga, demand to inspect documents and wallets for counterfeit bills, and pocket cash during the examination — typically stealing whatever notes are loose in a victim's wallet before issuing a fake receipt and disappearing.

scams.name: Beach Distraction Theft
scams.description:
You spread your towel on Playa El Rodadero, set your bag beside it, and wade into the water. A man walks past your belongings looking at his phone. Another sits nearby under an umbrella. The beach is busy and the atmosphere relaxed — the arrangement looks completely normal.

A vendor wades toward you in the shallows offering cold drinks and sunglasses, drawing your gaze away from shore. Or a beach ball lands near your bag, sparking a brief moment of noise. In that window — sometimes fewer than fifteen seconds — the first person has unzipped your bag, removed your phone and wallet, and moved away casually. By the time you return to your towel, nothing looks obviously disturbed.

Never leave electronics or cash in a bag on the sand — everything valuable either comes into the water with you in a waterproof pouch or stays at the hotel. When swimming with a companion, take turns in the water so one person always has eyes on the bags. At Tayrona, bring only what you need for the day: small cash for food and sunscreen, nothing you cannot afford to lose.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — bring only what you need for the day and leave everything else at the hotel Use a waterproof phone pouch that you can take into the water with you Take turns swimming with a travel companion so someone always watches the belongings Use a portable beach safe or lockbox that you can secure to a fixed object like a beach chair At Tayrona Park or Taganga, bring only essentials: cash for food, a cheap phone, and sunscreen
scams.location: Playa El Rodadero, Taganga Beach, Playa Blanca, and beach areas around Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona
scams.tldr: Teams of two to three people work Santa Marta's beaches — El Rodadero, Taganga, and Tayrona — using a staged vendor approach or a brief commotion to pull your attention away from the shore while an accomplice rifles through unattended bags, typically stealing phones, wallets, and cameras in under twenty seconds.

scams.name: Scopolamine (Devil's Breath) Drink Spiking
scams.description:
You are at a bar in El Rodadero when an attractive person strikes up a conversation. They speak good English, seem genuinely interested, and offer to buy you a drink. The encounter feels like one of those lucky travel nights — an unexpected connection in a coastal city.

The drink tastes completely normal. Within twenty minutes you feel dizzy and unusually agreeable. You do not resist when your new acquaintance suggests going back to your hotel. The next morning you wake up alone with no memory of how you got there. Your phone, wallet, watch, and laptop are gone. The drug was scopolamine — a plant-derived compound that blocks memory formation and makes victims cooperative. It can be dissolved in a drink, rubbed on paper, or blown as powder into a face.

Never leave your drink unattended and never accept a drink you did not watch being poured — if you stepped away from your glass even briefly, order a new one. Avoid bringing people you met at a bar or through a dating app back to your hotel room, especially if they push to leave quickly after meeting. If you feel suddenly dizzy or disoriented after one drink, tell someone you trust and get to a safe, public location immediately.
scams.avoidance: Never accept drinks from strangers and never leave your drink unattended — get a new one if you stepped away Avoid bringing strangers to your hotel room, especially people met at bars or through dating apps Go out with trusted friends and watch out for each other — if someone seems suddenly out of it, get them to safety immediately Use drink covers or bottle toppers to prevent anything being dropped into your beverage If you feel suddenly disoriented after a drink, tell a trusted person immediately and get to a safe location
scams.location: Bars and nightclubs in El Rodadero, late-night establishments in the Centro Histórico, and encounters initiated through dating apps
scams.tldr: Criminals in Santa Marta's El Rodadero bars and through dating apps drug tourists with scopolamine — known locally as burundanga — a colorless, odorless substance that causes total compliance and memory loss, then strip victims of phones, wallets, watches, and laptops while they are incapacitated, with no memory of what happened.

scams.name: Overpriced Unofficial Tour Guide
scams.description:
You arrive at the Tayrona National Park entrance and a man approaches immediately. He speaks confidently, knows the trail names, and quotes a price of 80,000 pesos for a private guided tour. For the Lost City trek, a similar pitch happens at hostels and bus stops in Santa Marta — someone offering a lower price than the licensed agencies, with vague promises of a 'better experience.'

Once inside the park, the guide checks his phone, rushes through the trails without explanation, and skips the main viewpoints. He brings you to the first beach and announces the tour is over. Back at the entrance you learn that self-guided entry was only 20,000 pesos and licensed Tayrona guides charge 50,000–60,000 through the park tourism office. For the Lost City, only five companies are authorized to run the four-day trek — anyone outside those operators is unlicensed and their permits are often invalid.

Book any Santa Marta tour through a licensed agency with verifiable reviews on TripAdvisor or GetYourGuide before you arrive — not from someone who approaches you at a park entrance. For the Lost City trek, the only authorized operators are Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, Magic Tour, and Adventure Colombia. Always ask for the guide's official certification and verify it with the park information desk if in doubt.
scams.avoidance: Book tours through licensed agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor, Google, or GetYourGuide For the Lost City trek, only book with one of the few licensed operators (Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour) Ask for official guide credentials and verify them with the tourism office if in doubt Get a written agreement including the itinerary, inclusions, and refund policy before paying Research the standard price for any tour before arriving so you can spot both overcharging and suspiciously low offers
scams.location: Outside the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona, Minca coffee farm tours, Lost City (Ciudad Perdida) trek departures, and around Santa Marta's harbor
scams.tldr: Unlicensed touts at the entrance to Tayrona National Park and along Lost City trek departure points offer guided tours for 60,000–80,000 pesos, deliver almost no service inside the park, then declare the tour finished at the first beach — while self-guided entry costs only 20,000 pesos and licensed guides charge 50,000–60,000 through the official park office.

scams.name: Bird Poop and Bracelet Distraction Theft
scams.description:
You are walking along the street near the cathedral when someone taps your shoulder and points urgently at a white substance on your jacket. It looks like bird droppings. A second person immediately materializes with napkins, apologizing and dabbing at the stain. The interaction feels like a genuine act of local kindness — people helping a tourist with an embarrassing mess.

While the napkin-holder leans toward your jacket, a third person has positioned themselves behind you. In the time it takes you to look down and assess the damage, your phone has been lifted from a pocket or your bag has been unzipped and relieved of its contents. In the bracelet variant, someone ties a colorful wristband on your wrist as a 'free gift' and immediately demands 50,000–100,000 pesos. While you argue about the price, accomplices work the crowd around you.

If anyone points out a stain on your clothing, do not stop — keep walking to a safe area before you look down to inspect it. Decline any unsolicited gift, bracelet, or flyer from someone on the street. In the Centro Histórico, wear your bag across your front and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket rather than a back pocket or an open compartment.
scams.avoidance: If someone points out a stain, do not stop — walk away to a safe area before inspecting your clothing Do not accept 'free' bracelets, flowers, or gifts from strangers — decline firmly and keep walking Wear your bag on your front in the Centro Histórico and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket Travel with a companion when possible so someone can watch your back during unexpected interactions Be especially alert near the cathedral and Parque de los Novios where these teams operate most actively
scams.location: Centro Histórico around the cathedral, Parque de los Novios, beachfront promenades, and busy pedestrian streets near Rodadero
scams.tldr: Teams of two to four people work Santa Marta's Centro Histórico and Parque de los Novios promenades using a staged bird-poop stain or a 'free' bracelet tying to distract tourists while accomplices pick pockets or unzip bags — typically stealing phones and cash within seconds of the distraction starting.

scams.name: Attempted Knifepoint Robbery Near Historic Center
scams.description:
You finish dinner near Parque de los Novios and decide to walk back to your hotel. The main plaza looks fine — busy, well lit, families out late. You take a shortcut through a side street to save five minutes. The block is quiet, but it does not look dangerous.

Two young men appear from a doorway twenty meters ahead. One pulls out a knife and demands your phone, your wallet, and your watch in rapid-fire Spanish. The entire interaction lasts under a minute. If you freeze or reach into your pocket too slowly, the threat escalates. Santa Marta's risk is concentrated in the transitional zones between bars and hotels — not the main plazas themselves, but the dark side streets connecting them.

After dark, take a taxi or ride-hailing app even for a one-block trip — never walk side streets at night, even ones that look short and quiet. If confronted, hand over your belongings immediately without resistance. Before going out, ask your hotel staff which specific streets are safe to walk after dark and which to avoid — that local knowledge is your most reliable map.
scams.avoidance: Never walk on side streets in Santa Marta after dark — use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi even for short distances Stick to well-lit, well-trafficked streets like Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios area when out at night Do not wear expensive jewelry, watches, or visible electronics when walking around the city If confronted, hand over your belongings without resistance — nothing is worth your safety Ask your hotel which specific streets are safe to walk at night and which to avoid
scams.location: Side streets off the Centro Histórico at night, dark streets near Taganga, and poorly lit areas between bars and hotels
scams.tldr: Armed robbers target tourists walking the side streets adjacent to Santa Marta's Centro Histórico and Taganga after dark — demanding phones, wallets, and watches at knifepoint in under a minute, with the threat escalating quickly if victims hesitate or resist.
